interview.q: What is the difference between a database and a schema?
interview.answer: A database is a separate catalog with its own connections; a schema is a namespace inside a database that groups objects.

interview.q: Why can CREATE DATABASE not run in a transaction?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL does not allow database creation inside a transaction block, so it cannot be rolled back like a table change.

interview.q: What is template1 vs template0?
interview.answer: template1 is the default template and may carry local customizations; template0 is pristine and is the safe base when changing encoding or locale.

interview.q: Who owns a newly created database?
interview.answer: The role that created it, unless OWNER is specified.

interview.q: Why does database encoding matter?
interview.answer: Encoding determines which characters can be stored and how text is represented; UTF8 is the usual choice for multilingual data.

interview.q: What are PostgreSQL identifier rules?
interview.answer: Unquoted identifiers fold to lowercase, are limited to 63 bytes and must not be empty; reserved words need quoting.

interview.q: What does CREATE TABLE define?
interview.answer: Ordered columns, their data types, defaults and constraints, plus table-level constraints and storage options.

interview.q: What does a primary key guarantee?
interview.answer: Uniqueness and non-nullness for the key columns, backed by a unique index.

interview.q: Does a foreign key require a unique parent key?
interview.answer: Yes. The referenced columns must be a primary key or have a unique constraint.

interview.q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
interview.answer: When the parent row is deleted, matching child rows are deleted automatically.

interview.q: What is the difference between SERIAL and IDENTITY?
interview.answer: SERIAL is a legacy pseudo-type that creates a sequence and default; GENERATED AS IDENTITY is standard SQL and preferred for new tables.

interview.q: What is the difference between CTAS and CREATE TABLE LIKE?
interview.answer: CTAS copies columns and rows from a query but not most constraints; LIKE copies the structure and can include constraints but no rows.

interview.q: Why is IF NOT EXISTS not a migration tool?
interview.answer: It only checks the relation name; it does not add missing columns or reconcile a different definition.

interview.q: What is search_path?
interview.answer: The ordered list of schemas PostgreSQL uses to resolve unqualified object names.

interview.q: How do you inspect a table in psql?
interview.answer: Use \d table for columns, indexes and constraints; \d+ adds storage and description details.

interview.q: What are common CREATE TABLE errors?
interview.answer: Relation already exists, duplicate column, missing type, invalid default, missing referenced table and permission denied.

interview.q: Why qualify table names with a schema?
interview.answer: Qualification removes ambiguity and protects against a hostile or unexpected search_path.

interview.q: What is a composite primary key?
interview.answer: A primary key made of two or more columns; the combination must be unique and none may be null.

interview.q: Does CTAS copy indexes?
interview.answer: No. CTAS creates a new table and data; indexes and most constraints must be added separately.

interview.q: What privilege is needed to create tables?
interview.answer: CREATE on the schema, plus USAGE on that schema; the role also needs a database connection.

logic.q: Why can CREATE DATABASE not be rolled back?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL forbids it inside a transaction block, so there is no transaction to roll back.

logic.q: Why do unquoted names fold to lowercase?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL normalizes unquoted identifiers to lowercase; quoted names preserve case.

logic.q: Why is 63 bytes the identifier limit?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL stores names in a fixed 64-byte field, leaving one byte for the terminator.

logic.q: Why use a schema instead of many databases?
logic.answer: Schemas share one database and connection while still namespacing objects, which simplifies backups and cross-schema queries.

logic.q: Why does a primary key create an index?
logic.answer: The unique index enforces uniqueness and speeds up lookups by key.

logic.q: Why must a foreign key parent exist first?
logic.answer: The referenced table and key must exist when the constraint is created.

logic.q: Why does CTAS not copy constraints?
logic.answer: It creates a new relation from a query result; constraints are not part of the query output.

logic.q: Why does LIKE copy no rows?
logic.answer: LIKE copies the table definition only; data must be inserted separately.

logic.q: Why is IF NOT EXISTS unsafe for migrations?
logic.answer: It silently accepts an existing table even if its columns or constraints differ from what the script expects.

logic.q: Why should search_path start with trusted schemas?
logic.answer: An attacker who can create objects in an earlier schema could shadow functions or tables.

logic.q: Why prefer IDENTITY over SERIAL?
logic.answer: IDENTITY is standard SQL, has explicit sequence ownership and avoids legacy pseudo-type behavior.

logic.q: Why add NOT NULL and DEFAULT together?
logic.answer: The column is always present and gets a value when the insert omits it.

logic.q: Why does a CHECK constraint allow NULL?
logic.answer: A CHECK passes when the predicate is true or NULL; add NOT NULL if NULL must be rejected.

logic.q: Why is ON DELETE CASCADE risky?
logic.answer: One parent delete can remove many child rows; use it only for true ownership relationships.

logic.q: Why inspect a table after DDL?
logic.answer: The actual columns, defaults and constraints are the source of truth; the script may have skipped or altered something.

modules.title: INSERT Statement
modules.goal: Write safe, correct INSERTs and handle conflicts deliberately.

topics.title: What Is INSERT?
topics.simple: INSERT table me naya row add karta hai.
topics.pro: INSERT is DML that adds one or more rows to a table, checks every constraint and returns a command tag such as INSERT 0 1.
points: INSERT changes data, not structure.
Every row must satisfy the table constraints.
A failed multi-row INSERT adds no rows from that statement.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Aarav', 82);

topics.title: INSERT INTO Syntax
topics.simple: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values) — yahi basic shape hai.
topics.pro: The general form is INSERT INTO table (column list) VALUES (row), (row), ... with an optional RETURNING clause.
points: Name the target columns explicitly.
The value count must match the column count.
Strings use single quotes.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Meera', 91);

topics.title: Inserting a Single Row
topics.simple: Ek row ke liye ek VALUES group likho.
topics.pro: A single-row INSERT supplies one parenthesized value list and inserts exactly one row or fails atomically.
points: One row is one VALUES group.
Constraints are checked before the row is stored.
The command tag reports 1 inserted row.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Kabir', 67);

topics.title: Inserting Multiple Rows
topics.simple: Ek hi INSERT me comma se multiple rows daal sakte hain.
topics.pro: A multi-row INSERT uses several VALUES groups in one statement, which is faster than many separate round trips and is atomic for the statement.
points: Each group needs the same column count.
One bad row fails the whole statement.
The tag reports the number of inserted rows.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Isha', 88), ('Zoya', 74), ('Dev', 59);

topics.title: Inserting Specific Columns
topics.simple: Jin columns ki value hai unka naam likho; baaki defaults ya NULL lete hain.
topics.pro: Listing only the columns you supply lets defaults, identity values and nullable columns fill the rest.
points: Omitted identity columns are generated.
Omitted nullable columns become NULL.
Omitted columns with defaults use the default.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('Anaya');

topics.title: Column Order and VALUES
topics.simple: Bina column list ke VALUES table ke column order par depend karta hai — ye fragile hai.
topics.pro: INSERT INTO table VALUES (...) maps values by the table’s physical column order; adding or reordering a column can silently break the statement.
points: Prefer an explicit column list.
Column order changes are migrations.
A count mismatch raises an error.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (1, 'Rohan', 'rohan@example.com', 77);

topics.title: DEFAULT VALUES
topics.simple: Agar har column ka default ya identity ho, to DEFAULT VALUES se khali row banao.
topics.pro: INSERT INTO table DEFAULT VALUES inserts a row using every column’s default; it fails if a required column has no default.
points: Useful for all-default settings rows.
Identity columns generate automatically.
A NOT NULL column without a default rejects it.

example.sql: INSERT INTO settings DEFAULT VALUES;

topics.title: NULL Values and Defaults
topics.simple: NULL ka matlab unknown value hai; DEFAULT ka matlab column ka predefined value.
topics.pro: NULL is an explicit unknown value, while DEFAULT asks PostgreSQL to use the column default; they are not interchangeable.
points: NULL is not an empty string or zero.
DEFAULT in VALUES uses the column default.
NOT NULL rejects an explicit NULL.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Meera', NULL);

topics.title: RETURNING
topics.simple: RETURNING inserted row ki values wapas deta hai — jaise naya id.
topics.pro: RETURNING returns rows produced by the INSERT, including generated identity values and defaults, in the same statement.
points: RETURNING is PostgreSQL syntax.
It avoids a second SELECT for the new id.
RETURNING * returns every inserted column.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Aarav', 82) RETURNING id, name;

topics.title: INSERT INTO SELECT
topics.simple: Ek query ka result doosri table me insert kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: INSERT INTO target (columns) SELECT ... copies rows from a query; the selected columns must match the target list in number and compatible types.
points: It can insert zero rows.
Constraints are checked per row.
ORDER BY and LIMIT can shape the source.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students_backup (name, marks) SELECT name, marks FROM students;

topics.title: Inserting From a Query with All Columns
topics.simple: Agar dono tables ka structure same hai to SELECT * se copy kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: INSERT INTO target SELECT * FROM source works only when column order, count and types line up; explicit columns are safer across schema changes.
points: SELECT * depends on both table shapes.
A column added to one table breaks the copy.
Prefer naming the columns.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students_backup SELECT * FROM students;

topics.title: Identity Columns and INSERT
topics.simple: Identity column khud value banata hai; explicit value dene par rules hain.
topics.pro: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY rejects explicit values unless OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is used; GENERATED BY DEFAULT accepts them.
points: Let the database generate ids.
Use OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE only for migrations.
SERIAL is the legacy alternative.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (id, name) OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE VALUES (10, 'Kabir');

topics.title: Handling Duplicate Rows with ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
topics.simple: Duplicate unique value aaye to ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING us row ko skip kar deta hai.
topics.pro: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING suppresses a unique or exclusion violation for the targeted conflict and inserts the remaining rows.
points: The conflict target must match a unique constraint.
Skipped rows are not returned by RETURNING.
Without a target it handles any conflict.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (email, name) VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Aarav') ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING;

topics.title: Upsert with ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
topics.simple: Conflict aaye to naya row insert karne ke bajaye existing row update kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: ON CONFLICT (target) DO UPDATE SET ... performs an upsert; EXCLUDED holds the proposed row values.
points: The target needs a unique constraint.
EXCLUDED refers to the row you tried to insert.
Do not hit the same row twice in one statement.

example.sql:
INSERT INTO students (email, name, marks) VALUES ('a@example.com', 'Aarav S', 90)
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name, marks = EXCLUDED.marks;

topics.title: INSERT Errors and Constraints
topics.simple: INSERT fail hota hai jab NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FOREIGN KEY ya type violate ho.
topics.pro: Constraint violations abort the statement: not-null, unique, check, foreign key, invalid input syntax and value too long are the common failures.
points: Read the constraint name in the error.
One failed statement adds no rows.
Fix the value, not the constraint, unless the rule is wrong.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (NULL);
example.output: ERROR: null value in column "name" violates not-null constraint

topics.title: Safe Insertion and Transactions
topics.simple: Important inserts ko transaction me karo taaki failure par rollback ho sake.
topics.pro: Wrap related inserts in BEGIN ... COMMIT; an error aborts the transaction and ROLLBACK discards every uncommitted change.
points: Test on sample data first.
Commit only when the whole unit is correct.
Use savepoints for partial recovery.

topics.title: Bulk Insert Performance
topics.simple: Bahut rows ke liye multi-row INSERT ya COPY use karo; ek-ek INSERT slow hota hai.
topics.pro: Multi-row VALUES reduces round trips; COPY is the fastest bulk-load path for large files, at the cost of fewer per-row controls.
points: Batch hundreds of rows per statement.
COPY is a utility command.
Indexes and triggers still cost time per row.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('A', 60), ('B', 70), ('C', 80);

topics.title: INSERT ... RETURNING Generated IDs
topics.simple: Naya id chahiye to RETURNING id use karo — alag SELECT ki zaroorat nahi.
topics.pro: RETURNING id captures generated identity values for each inserted row, including multi-row inserts.
points: The order of returned rows follows insertion order in practice.
RETURNING can return defaults too.
Do not assume ids are contiguous.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES ('Isha'), ('Dev') RETURNING id;

topics.title: INSERT Best Practices
topics.simple: Columns name karo, values validate karo aur bulk operations batch me karo.
topics.pro: Production INSERTs name columns, supply typed values, handle conflicts deliberately, batch where useful and run inside a transaction when rows belong together.
points: Never rely on column order.
Do not hide every conflict with DO NOTHING.
Use RETURNING for generated values.

example.sql: INSERT INTO students (name, marks) VALUES ('Anaya', 95) RETURNING id, name, marks;

topics.title: Practical Student Enrollment Insert
topics.simple: Students aur enrollments me related rows ek transaction me daalo.
topics.pro: A real enrollment flow inserts the student, captures the generated id with RETURNING, then inserts the enrollment row in the same transaction.
points: The parent row must exist before the child.
Use the returned id, not a guessed one.
Commit only after both inserts succeed.

interview.q: What is INSERT?
interview.answer: DML that adds one or more rows to a table and checks every constraint.

interview.q: What is the basic INSERT syntax?
interview.answer: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values); with optional RETURNING.

interview.q: How do you insert multiple rows?
interview.answer: Use multiple comma-separated VALUES groups in one INSERT.

interview.q: Why is an explicit column list recommended?
interview.answer: It is independent of physical column order and keeps working when unrelated columns are added.

interview.q: What happens if the column count and value count differ?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL raises a syntax error; the statement inserts nothing.

interview.q: What does DEFAULT VALUES do?
interview.answer: Inserts one row using every column default; it fails if a required column has no default.

interview.q: What is the difference between NULL and DEFAULT in VALUES?
interview.answer: NULL stores an unknown value; DEFAULT asks for the column default.

interview.q: What does RETURNING do?
interview.answer: Returns inserted rows, including generated ids and defaults, in the same statement.

interview.q: How does INSERT INTO SELECT work?
interview.answer: It inserts the rows produced by a SELECT; the target and source columns must match in number and compatible types.

interview.q: What is an identity column?
interview.answer: A column whose value is generated from an attached sequence; GENERATED ALWAYS is the standard form.

interview.q: How do you insert an explicit value into GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY?
interview.answer: Add OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE to the INSERT; use it only for migrations or imports.

interview.q: What does ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING do?
interview.answer: Skips a row that would violate the targeted unique or exclusion constraint.

interview.q: What does ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE do?
interview.answer: Performs an upsert: updates the existing row with values from the proposed row.

interview.answer: A pseudo-table holding the values proposed by the INSERT, used in the DO UPDATE SET clause.

interview.q: What is a common INSERT error?

interview.q: Why use a transaction for related inserts?

interview.answer: It returns generated ids immediately, avoiding a race-prone follow-up SELECT.

interview.q: What is an upsert?
interview.answer: Insert a row, or update the existing row when a unique conflict occurs.

logic.q: Why is an explicit column list safer than relying on column order?
logic.answer: Adding or reordering a column changes the physical order; an explicit list keeps the statement correct.

logic.q: Why is a multi-row INSERT faster than many single-row INSERTs?
logic.answer: It sends one statement and one round trip instead of many network and planning cycles.

logic.q: Why does one bad row fail a multi-row INSERT?
logic.answer: The statement is atomic; a constraint violation aborts the whole statement.

logic.q: Why is NULL different from DEFAULT?
logic.answer: NULL stores an unknown value; DEFAULT asks PostgreSQL to apply the column default.

logic.q: Why does DEFAULT VALUES fail on a NOT NULL column without a default?
logic.answer: There is no value to store, so the not-null constraint rejects the row.

logic.q: Why is RETURNING useful after an INSERT?
logic.answer: It returns generated ids and defaults without a second query or a race.

logic.q: Why does INSERT INTO SELECT need matching columns?
logic.answer: The selected values are mapped positionally to the target column list.

logic.q: Why does GENERATED ALWAYS reject an explicit id?
logic.answer: ALWAYS protects the sequence-generated value; OVERRIDING SYSTEM VALUE is the deliberate escape hatch.

logic.q: Why does ON CONFLICT need a unique constraint?
logic.answer: PostgreSQL must know which conflict the target identifies; without a matching unique or exclusion constraint it cannot arbitrate.

logic.q: Why can ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE affect one row twice?
logic.answer: If the proposed rows contain the same conflict key twice, PostgreSQL cannot update the same existing row twice and raises an error.

logic.q: Why is DO NOTHING dangerous as a default?
logic.answer: It silently hides data-quality problems that should be fixed or reported.

logic.q: Why use a transaction for a student plus enrollment?
logic.answer: The two rows belong together; a failure in the second should not leave a half-written flow.

logic.q: Why is COPY faster than INSERT for bulk data?
logic.answer: COPY streams rows with far less per-row overhead and fewer round trips.

logic.q: Why can INSERT fire triggers?
logic.answer: Row-level INSERT triggers run for each inserted row; they are part of the write cost.

logic.q: Why should you not assume generated ids are contiguous?
logic.answer: Rolled-back inserts and sequences can leave gaps; ids are unique, not gapless.

modules.title: SELECT Statement
modules.goal: Read and shape result sets with correct projection and expressions.

topics.title: Introduction to SELECT
topics.simple: SELECT database se data padhne ka command hai — jo columns chahiye, wo choose karta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT is DQL that projects a result set from one or more relations, evaluates expressions and returns rows without modifying stored data.
points: SELECT is read-only.
It can return zero, one or many rows.
The result columns are defined by the select list.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students;
example.output: One row per student with name and marks.

topics.title: Basic SELECT Syntax
topics.simple: Basic shape: SELECT columns FROM table.
topics.pro: The core syntax is SELECT select_list FROM relation [WHERE ...] [ORDER BY ...] [LIMIT ...]; the select list defines the output columns.
points: The select list comes first.
FROM names the source relation.
Clauses have a fixed order.

example.sql: SELECT id, name FROM students;

topics.title: SELECT *
topics.simple: SELECT * table ke saare columns deta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT * expands to every column in the relation at planning time; it is convenient for exploration but fragile in production.
points: It returns every column, including future ones.
Column order follows the table definition.
Avoid it in application queries.

example.sql: SELECT * FROM students;
example.output: Every column and row from students.

topics.title: Selecting Specific Columns
topics.simple: Sirf zaroori columns choose karo — network aur result chhota rehta hai.
topics.pro: A projection list names the columns to return; omitted columns are not read into the result, which can reduce I/O and payload.
points: Name each column explicitly.
The output order is the list order.
Fewer columns is usually cheaper.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students;

topics.title: Selecting Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Comma se multiple columns likho.
topics.pro: Multiple columns are separated by commas and appear in the same order as the select list, regardless of table order.
points: Commas separate expressions.
A trailing comma is a syntax error.
Duplicate expressions are allowed.

example.sql: SELECT id, name, email, marks FROM students;

topics.title: Column Aliases
topics.simple: Alias result column ka temporary naam hota hai.
topics.pro: An alias renames a result column for the query output; it does not rename the underlying table column.
points: Aliases improve report readability.
The AS keyword is optional.
Aliases are not visible in WHERE in PostgreSQL.

example.sql: SELECT name AS student_name, marks AS score FROM students;

topics.title: AS Keyword
topics.simple: AS alias ko explicit banata hai — padhne me clear.
topics.pro: AS introduces a column or table alias; it is optional for column aliases but required for some derived-table aliases.
points: AS is optional for column aliases.
Quoted aliases preserve case and spaces.
Aliases last for the query only.

example.sql: SELECT name AS "Student Name" FROM students;

topics.title: Calculated Columns
topics.simple: SELECT me expression se naya column bana sakte hain.
topics.pro: The select list can contain expressions, not just columns; each expression becomes an output column with a computed value per row.
points: Calculations do not change stored data.
Use an alias to name the result.
The expression is evaluated per row.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks + 5 AS boosted FROM students;

topics.title: Arithmetic Operations
topics.simple: SELECT me +, -, *, /, % use kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: Arithmetic operators follow standard precedence; integer division truncates, while a numeric operand keeps the fraction.
points: * and / bind tighter than + and -.
Use parentheses to force order.
Integer / integer truncates.

example.sql: SELECT 7 / 2 AS int_div, ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1) AS num_div;

topics.title: Concatenating Columns
topics.simple: || operator strings ko jodta hai.
topics.pro: The || operator concatenates text; cast non-text values explicitly when the result must be predictable.
points: || is concatenation.
NULL concatenated with anything is NULL.
Cast numbers with ::text.

example.sql: SELECT name || ' scored ' || marks::text AS label FROM students;

topics.title: Selecting Expressions
topics.simple: SELECT me literals, functions aur arithmetic — sab expressions hain.
topics.pro: A select-list item can be a column, literal, function call or arithmetic expression; PostgreSQL names an unaliased expression ?column?.
points: Expressions can be nested.
Use aliases for stable column names.
Functions run per row unless aggregated.

example.sql: SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 AS result;

topics.title: SELECT DISTINCT
topics.simple: DISTINCT duplicate result rows hata deta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicate rows from the final result after projection; it applies to the whole select list, not to one column.
points: DISTINCT is applied after SELECT expressions.
It treats NULLs as equal for duplicate removal.
It can cost a sort or hash.

example.sql: SELECT DISTINCT marks FROM students;

topics.title: Duplicate Values
topics.simple: Table me same value kai rows me ho sakti hai; DISTINCT unhe ek baar dikhata hai.
topics.pro: Duplicates are normal in relational data unless a constraint forbids them; duplicate removal is a query-time decision, not a storage rule.
points: A primary key prevents duplicate rows by key.
Other columns can repeat.
DISTINCT changes the result, not the table.

example.sql: SELECT marks FROM students;

topics.title: DISTINCT with Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Multiple columns ke saath DISTINCT unique combinations deta hai.
topics.pro: SELECT DISTINCT a, b removes duplicate pairs; it does not return one row per distinct a.
points: The whole tuple is compared.
Column order does not change the set.
Use GROUP BY when you need aggregates per key.

example.sql: SELECT DISTINCT name, marks FROM students;

topics.title: Logical Query Order
topics.simple: SQL likhne ka order aur database ke evaluate karne ka order alag hai.
topics.pro: Logical evaluation is FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT, which explains alias visibility and filter timing.
points: WHERE runs before SELECT.
Aliases are available in ORDER BY.
LIMIT runs last.

example.sql: SELECT name AS n FROM students ORDER BY n;
example.output: Rows sorted by the alias n.

topics.title: Understanding Query Results
topics.simple: Result ek table jaisa hota hai — columns aur rows; zero rows bhi valid result hai.
topics.pro: A SELECT result is a relation with named columns and zero or more rows; an empty result is not an error and does not mean NULL.
points: Zero rows is a valid answer.
Column names come from the select list.
NULL is a value, not an empty result.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 100;

topics.title: SELECT Query Execution
topics.simple: Database query ko parse, plan aur execute karta hai.
topics.pro: The server parses the statement, rewrites it, plans access paths, then executes; EXPLAIN shows the plan without running the query.
points: Parsing checks syntax.
The planner chooses scans and joins.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM students WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Common SELECT Mistakes
topics.simple: Common galtiyan: galat column, missing comma, alias WHERE me use karna, integer division bhoolna.
topics.pro: Typical mistakes are misspelled columns, trailing commas, assuming alias visibility in WHERE, integer division and expecting DISTINCT to apply to one column.
points: Read the error position.
Check the select list commas.
Qualify ambiguous columns.

example.sql: SELECT names FROM students;

topics.title: SELECT Without FROM
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me FROM ke bina bhi expression select kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: SELECT without FROM evaluates the select list once and returns one row; it is useful for testing expressions and functions.
points: No table means one synthetic row.
It is PostgreSQL-compatible.
Aliases name the output.

example.sql: SELECT 1 + 1 AS answer;

topics.title: Practical Student Report Query
topics.simple: Ab columns, alias, calculation aur concatenation mila kar report banao.
topics.pro: A report query combines projection, aliases and expressions to produce a readable result without changing the table.
points: Name every output column.
Cast numbers before concatenation.
Keep the query deterministic.

example.sql: SELECT id, name AS student, marks, marks + 5 AS boosted, name || ' (' || marks::text || ')' AS label FROM students;
example.output: A table with id, student, marks, boosted and label columns.

learn.q: Which category does SELECT belong to?
learn.why: SELECT reads data; many curricula call that DQL.

learn.q: What does SELECT * return?
learn.why: * expands to every column at planning time.

learn.q: How do you return only name and marks?
learn.why: List the columns in the select list.

learn.q: Which keyword gives a result column a temporary name?
learn.why: AS introduces a column alias.

learn.q: Is AS required for a column alias?
learn.why: SELECT name n is a valid alias form.

learn.q: What does SELECT 7 / 2 return?
learn.why: Both operands are integers, so integer division truncates.

learn.q: What does ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1) return?
learn.why: 7.0 is numeric, so the division keeps the fraction, and ROUND fixes the display scale.

learn.q: Which operator concatenates text?
learn.why: PostgreSQL uses || for string concatenation.

learn.q: What does SELECT DISTINCT do?
learn.why: DISTINCT removes duplicate projected rows.

learn.q: Does DISTINCT apply to one column or the whole select list?
learn.why: The entire projected tuple is compared.

learn.q: Which clause runs first logically?
learn.why: The source rows are established before projection.

learn.q: Can a column alias be used in WHERE in PostgreSQL?
learn.why: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet.

learn.q: Can a column alias be used in ORDER BY?
learn.why: ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT, so aliases are available.

learn.q: Is SELECT 1; valid in PostgreSQL?
learn.why: SELECT without FROM evaluates the expression once.

learn.q: What is an unaliased expression column named?
learn.why: PostgreSQL uses ?column? when no alias is given.

learn.q: What does SELECT NULL return?
learn.why: NULL is a value, not an empty result.

learn.q: How many columns does SELECT name FROM students return?
learn.why: The select list has one item.

learn.q: What does SELECT 2 + 3 * 4 return?
learn.why: Multiplication binds tighter than addition.

learn.q: What does SELECT (2 + 3) * 4 return?
learn.why: Parentheses force the addition first.

learn.q: What does a SELECT returning zero rows mean?
learn.why: No matching rows is a normal result set.

interview.q: What is SELECT?
interview.answer: DQL that projects a result set from relations and expressions without changing stored rows.

interview.q: What is the basic SELECT syntax?
interview.answer: SELECT select_list FROM relation [WHERE ...] [ORDER BY ...] [LIMIT ...];

interview.q: What is the logical order of query evaluation?
interview.answer: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

interview.q: Why is SELECT * risky in production?
interview.answer: It returns every current and future column, can break consumers and transfers more data than needed.

interview.q: What is a column alias?
interview.answer: A temporary name for a result column; it does not rename the table column.

interview.q: Is AS required for an alias?
interview.answer: No, it is optional for column aliases, but it improves clarity.

interview.q: How do you preserve spaces or case in an alias?
interview.answer: Double-quote it, for example AS "Student Name".

interview.q: What is the difference between DISTINCT and GROUP BY?
interview.answer: DISTINCT removes duplicate projected rows; GROUP BY forms groups for aggregates and can be paired with HAVING.

interview.q: Does DISTINCT apply to one column or all selected columns?
interview.answer: All selected columns; the whole tuple is compared.

interview.q: How does DISTINCT treat NULL?
interview.answer: It treats NULLs as equal for duplicate removal, so one NULL survives.

interview.q: Why does 7 / 2 return 3?
interview.answer: Both operands are integers, so integer division truncates the fraction.

interview.q: How do you get 3.5 from 7 and 2?
interview.answer: Use a numeric operand and round the display, for example ROUND(7.0 / 2, 1). A bare numeric division can display extra scale digits.

interview.q: What does || do with NULL?
interview.answer: Concatenating NULL with anything returns NULL; use COALESCE if a fallback is needed.

interview.q: Why is an unaliased expression column called ?column??
interview.answer: PostgreSQL needs a name; without an alias it uses ?column? for the expression.

interview.q: Can SELECT run without FROM?
interview.answer: Yes. It evaluates the select list once and returns one row.

interview.q: Is SELECT read-only?
interview.answer: It does not change stored rows, though it can call functions; it is DQL.

interview.q: Why are aliases unavailable in WHERE?
interview.answer: Logical evaluation runs WHERE before SELECT, so the alias has not been defined yet.

interview.q: Why are aliases available in ORDER BY?
interview.answer: ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so the projected alias exists.

interview.q: What does an empty result set mean?
interview.answer: The query matched zero rows; it is not an error and not a NULL row.

interview.q: What is the difference between a column and an expression in SELECT?
interview.answer: A column reads a stored value; an expression computes a new value per row.

logic.q: Why can an alias not be used in WHERE?
logic.answer: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias has not been defined yet.

logic.q: Why is an alias available in ORDER BY?
logic.answer: ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT, so the projected alias exists.

logic.q: Why does DISTINCT apply to the whole select list?
logic.answer: It compares complete projected rows; there is no per-column mode.

logic.q: Why can SELECT * break an application?
logic.answer: A new column changes the result shape and can break consumers that expect a fixed set.

logic.q: Why does 7 / 2 return 3?
logic.answer: Both operands are integers, so integer division truncates.

logic.q: Why does 7.0 / 2 keep the fraction?
logic.answer: 7.0 is numeric, so the division uses numeric arithmetic.

logic.q: Why does NULL || text return NULL?
logic.answer: Concatenation with an unknown value is unknown; use COALESCE to supply a default.

logic.q: Why does multiplication run before addition?
logic.answer: SQL arithmetic gives * and / higher precedence than + and -.

logic.q: Why do parentheses matter in expressions?
logic.answer: They override precedence and make the intended grouping explicit.

logic.q: Why is an unaliased expression called ?column??
logic.answer: The result needs a name; PostgreSQL supplies a placeholder when none is given.

logic.q: Why is SELECT without FROM useful?
logic.answer: It evaluates expressions and functions once without needing a table.

logic.q: Why can DISTINCT be expensive?
logic.answer: It may sort or hash the whole result to find duplicates.

logic.q: Why does a zero-row result not mean NULL?
logic.answer: Zero rows is an empty relation; NULL is a value inside a row.

logic.q: Why quote an alias with spaces?
logic.answer: Unquoted identifiers cannot contain spaces and fold to lowercase; quotes preserve the exact text.

logic.q: Why are SQL keywords case-insensitive?
logic.answer: The parser normalizes keywords, so SELECT and select mean the same thing.

modules.title: WHERE Clause and Filtering
modules.goal: Write precise predicates and avoid NULL and precedence traps.

topics.title: Introduction to WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE rows ko filter karta hai — sirf matching rows result me aate hain.
topics.pro: WHERE is a row-level filter evaluated after FROM and before GROUP BY; it keeps only rows whose predicate is true.
points: WHERE works on individual rows.
False or unknown rows are removed.
It runs before aggregation.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Filtering Rows
topics.simple: Filter lagane se result chhota aur relevant hota hai.
topics.pro: A predicate is a boolean expression; rows with a true result pass, while false and NULL results are discarded.
points: A predicate returns true, false or unknown.
Unknown behaves like false for filtering.
Combine predicates for precise filters.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks >= 60;

topics.title: Equality (=)
topics.simple: = exact match check karta hai.
topics.pro: The equality operator compares two values and returns true only when they are equal; NULL never equals anything.
points: Use single quotes for strings.
Double quotes are identifiers, not strings.
Equality is case-sensitive for text.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav';

topics.title: Inequality (!= and <>)
topics.simple: Not equal ke liye <> ya != use karo.
topics.pro: Both <> and != mean not equal in PostgreSQL; <> is the SQL-standard spelling.
points: <> is portable.
!= is accepted by PostgreSQL.
NULL comparisons still return unknown.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks <> 80;

topics.title: Greater Than and Less Than
topics.simple: > bada aur < chhota compare karta hai.
topics.pro: > and < compare values using the type’s ordering; they work for numbers, dates and text under the database collation.
points: > is strict greater than.
< is strict less than.
Dates compare chronologically.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80;

topics.title: Greater Than or Equal and Less Than or Equal
topics.simple: >= aur <= boundary value ko bhi include karte hain.
topics.pro: >= keeps values greater than or equal to the boundary; <= keeps values less than or equal to it.
points: >= includes the boundary.
<= includes the boundary.
Combine both for a range.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 80;

topics.title: AND
topics.simple: AND tab true hota hai jab dono conditions true hon.
topics.pro: AND combines predicates with logical conjunction; both sides must be true for the row to pass.
points: AND is stricter than OR.
One false side rejects the row.
Parentheses clarify mixed logic.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 AND marks <= 90;

topics.title: OR
topics.simple: OR tab true hota hai jab koi ek condition true ho.
topics.pro: OR combines predicates with logical disjunction; at least one side must be true for the row to pass.
points: OR is broader than AND.
Two false sides reject the row.
NULL on both sides yields unknown.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera';

topics.title: NOT
topics.simple: NOT condition ko ulta karta hai.
topics.pro: NOT negates a boolean predicate; NOT true is false, NOT false is true and NOT unknown is unknown.
points: NOT is not the same as !=.
Negating a NULL predicate stays unknown.
Use parentheses after NOT.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE NOT (marks < 60);
example.output: Students with 60 or more, excluding NULL marks.

topics.title: Combining AND, OR and NOT
topics.simple: Mixed conditions me precedence aur parentheses bahut important hain.
topics.pro: Mixed predicates combine with NOT, AND and OR; AND binds tighter than OR, so parentheses should state the intended grouping.
points: AND runs before OR.
NOT applies to the expression that follows.
Parentheses prevent logic bugs.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera') AND marks > 80;

topics.title: BETWEEN and NOT BETWEEN
topics.simple: BETWEEN inclusive range check karta hai.
topics.pro: BETWEEN low AND high is inclusive on both ends; NOT BETWEEN keeps values outside the range.
points: Both boundaries are included.
Low must come first.
NOT BETWEEN excludes the range.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 60 AND 90;

topics.title: IN and NOT IN
topics.simple: IN list me se koi match check karta hai.
topics.pro: IN tests membership in a value list; NOT IN tests exclusion, with a dangerous NULL behaviour.
points: IN is shorthand for several ORs.
NOT IN with a NULL in the list returns no rows.
The list values must be comparable.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name IN ('Aarav', 'Meera', 'Kabir');

topics.title: LIKE and NOT LIKE
topics.simple: LIKE pattern matching karta hai, NOT LIKE ulta.
topics.pro: LIKE matches text against a pattern with % and _ wildcards; it is case-sensitive in PostgreSQL, while ILIKE is case-insensitive.
points: LIKE is case-sensitive.
NOT LIKE excludes matches.
Use ILIKE for case-insensitive matching.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE 'A%';

topics.title: Percent Wildcard
topics.simple: % kisi bhi length ke characters ko match karta hai.
topics.pro: The % wildcard matches zero or more characters in a LIKE pattern.
points: A% matches names starting with A.
%a% matches a anywhere.
A leading % usually prevents a plain index scan.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE '%a%';

topics.title: Underscore Wildcard
topics.simple: _ exactly ek character match karta hai.
topics.pro: The _ wildcard matches exactly one character, so it is useful for fixed-position patterns.
points: _ is one character.
% is any number.
Combine them for shape-based filters.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name LIKE '_a%';
example.output: Names whose second character is a.

topics.title: IS NULL
topics.simple: NULL check karne ke liye IS NULL use karo, = NULL nahi.
topics.pro: IS NULL is the only reliable null test; equality with NULL returns unknown and filters every row out.
points: NULL means unknown.
= NULL never matches.
IS NULL is the correct predicate.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email IS NULL;

topics.title: IS NOT NULL
topics.simple: IS NOT NULL aise rows deta hai jahan value present ho.
topics.pro: IS NOT NULL keeps rows where the column has a real value rather than NULL.
points: It is the negation of IS NULL.
It does not treat empty string as NULL.
Use it before comparing optional columns.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE email IS NOT NULL;

topics.title: Boolean Filtering
topics.simple: Boolean column ko seedha WHERE me use kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: A boolean column is itself a predicate; WHERE active keeps true, WHERE NOT active keeps false, and NULL is excluded from both.
points: WHERE active means true.
WHERE NOT active means false.
Use IS NOT TRUE to include NULL.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM users WHERE active;

topics.title: Operator Precedence
topics.simple: Comparison pehle, phir NOT, phir AND, phir OR.
topics.pro: Comparison operators bind tighter than NOT, NOT binds tighter than AND, and AND binds tighter than OR; rely on parentheses when mixing.
points: AND beats OR.
NOT applies before AND.
Comparison is evaluated first.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 80 OR name = 'Aarav' AND marks > 60;

topics.title: Parentheses
topics.simple: Parentheses se condition ka group clear karo.
topics.pro: Parentheses override precedence and make the intended logic readable; they are the cheapest way to prevent a filter bug.
points: Group OR before AND when needed.
Parenthesize NOT.
Readable logic is reviewable logic.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name = 'Aarav' OR name = 'Meera') AND marks > 80;

topics.title: Case Sensitivity and ILIKE
topics.simple: PostgreSQL text comparison case-sensitive hai; ILIKE case-insensitive match deta hai.
topics.pro: LIKE and = compare text case-sensitively under the collation; ILIKE lowercases both sides for matching, and LOWER(name) is the portable alternative.
points: = is case-sensitive.
ILIKE is PostgreSQL-specific.
LOWER() can match but may not use a plain index.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE name ILIKE 'aarav';

topics.title: Escaping Wildcards
topics.simple: Literal % ya _ match karna ho to ESCAPE use karo.
topics.pro: A backslash escapes % and _ in a LIKE pattern when ESCAPE is declared; without escaping, the wildcard keeps its special meaning.
points: Escape % as \%.
Escape _ as \_.
Declare ESCAPE explicitly for clarity.

example.sql: SELECT code FROM items WHERE code LIKE 'A\_%' ESCAPE '\';
example.output: Codes starting with the literal A_.

topics.title: Complex WHERE Conditions
topics.simple: Real filters me multiple AND, OR, IN, LIKE aur NULL checks combine hote hain.
topics.pro: A complex predicate should be built in layers: isolate each rule, parenthesize OR groups, and test the row count before trusting the result.
points: Write one rule at a time.
Parenthesize mixed AND/OR.
Use IS NULL explicitly.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE (name LIKE 'A%' OR name LIKE 'M%') AND marks BETWEEN 60 AND 95 AND email IS NOT NULL;
example.output: Matching names with marks in range and a known email.

topics.title: Practical Student Filtering
topics.simple: Ab multiple filters ko mila kar ek useful student report banao.
topics.pro: A production filter combines range, membership, pattern and null checks while keeping each predicate readable and index-friendly.
points: Filter on selective columns first.
Avoid leading wildcards on large tables.
Verify the row count before shipping.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks BETWEEN 70 AND 90 AND name LIKE 'A%' AND email IS NOT NULL ORDER BY marks DESC;
example.output: Students in range whose name starts with A and have an email.

interview.q: What is WHERE?
interview.answer: A row-level filter evaluated after FROM and before GROUP BY; only rows whose predicate is true pass.

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after aggregation.

interview.q: What comparison operators does SQL provide?
interview.answer: =, <>, !=, >, <, >= and <=, plus BETWEEN, IN, LIKE and IS NULL predicates.

interview.q: What is the difference between <> and !=?
interview.answer: Both mean not equal in PostgreSQL; <> is the SQL-standard spelling.

interview.q: Is BETWEEN inclusive?
interview.answer: Yes, both the low and high boundaries are included.

interview.q: What is IN equivalent to?
interview.answer: A chain of OR equality comparisons, such as x = a OR x = b.

interview.q: Why is NOT IN with NULL dangerous?
interview.answer: Every comparison with NULL is unknown, so the NOT IN predicate can return no rows unexpectedly.

interview.q: What is the difference between LIKE and ILIKE?
interview.answer: LIKE is case-sensitive; ILIKE is case-insensitive in PostgreSQL.

interview.q: What do % and _ mean in LIKE?
interview.answer: % matches any sequence of characters; _ matches exactly one character.

interview.q: How do you match a literal % or _?
interview.answer: Escape it with a backslash and declare ESCAPE, for example LIKE A\_% ESCAPE '\'.

interview.q: How do you test for NULL?
interview.answer: Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL; = NULL never matches.

interview.q: What is three-valued logic?
interview.answer: SQL predicates can be true, false or unknown; unknown arises from NULL comparisons and is filtered like false.

interview.q: How does WHERE treat a boolean column?
interview.answer: The column is itself the predicate: WHERE active keeps true rows.

interview.q: How do you include false and NULL boolean rows?
interview.answer: Use WHERE active IS NOT TRUE; WHERE NOT active keeps only false.

interview.q: What is the precedence of NOT, AND and OR?
interview.answer: NOT binds tighter than AND, and AND binds tighter than OR.

interview.q: Why use parentheses?
interview.answer: They override precedence and document the intended grouping.

interview.q: Can a SELECT alias be used in WHERE?
interview.answer: No, because WHERE is evaluated before SELECT.

interview.q: Can WHERE use functions?
interview.answer: Yes, but a function on a column can prevent a plain index scan.

interview.q: Why can a leading % hurt performance?
interview.answer: It prevents a normal B-tree index scan because the pattern has no fixed prefix.

interview.q: How do you filter a date range?
interview.answer: Use >= start AND < next_day for a half-open range, or BETWEEN for inclusive dates.

logic.q: Why does name = NULL return no rows?
logic.answer: Equality with an unknown value is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true rows.

logic.q: Why does NOT IN (1, NULL) return no rows?
logic.answer: Each comparison against NULL is unknown, so the NOT IN predicate never becomes true.

logic.q: Why does AND bind tighter than OR?
logic.answer: SQL gives AND higher precedence, so a OR b AND c means a OR (b AND c).

logic.q: Why use parentheses even when precedence is known?
logic.answer: They document intent and prevent a later edit from changing the logic.

logic.q: Why is BETWEEN inclusive?
logic.answer: It expands to low <= x AND x <= high, including both boundaries.

logic.q: Why is LIKE case-sensitive?
logic.answer: It compares text under the collation without case folding; ILIKE performs the case-insensitive match.

logic.q: Why can ILIKE be slower?
logic.answer: It cannot use a plain B-tree index on the original text; it may need a scan or a special index.

logic.q: Why can LOWER(name) prevent an index scan?
logic.answer: A plain index on name does not index LOWER(name); use an expression index if needed.

logic.q: Why does WHERE active exclude NULL?
logic.answer: A NULL boolean is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true.

logic.q: Why does IS NOT TRUE include NULL?
logic.answer: It is true for both false and unknown values.

logic.q: Why does a leading % hurt performance?
logic.answer: The pattern has no fixed prefix, so a normal B-tree cannot seek to a starting point.

logic.q: Why does _ match exactly one character?
logic.answer: It is the single-character wildcard in LIKE patterns.

logic.q: Why use ESCAPE?
logic.answer: It tells LIKE which character makes the next wildcard literal.

logic.q: Why can a SELECT alias not be used in WHERE?
logic.answer: WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, so the alias does not exist yet.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before GROUP BY?
logic.answer: Rows are filtered first, then the surviving rows are grouped and aggregated.

modules.title: ORDER BY, LIMIT and OFFSET
modules.goal: Produce deterministic sorted pages and top-N reports.

topics.title: Introduction to ORDER BY
topics.simple: ORDER BY result rows ko sort karta hai.
topics.pro: ORDER BY sorts the final result set using one or more sort expressions; it runs after SELECT and DISTINCT and before LIMIT.
points: No ORDER BY means no guaranteed order.
ASC is the default.
Sorting happens after filtering.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Sorting Rows
topics.simple: Sorting se rows ek predictable sequence me aate hain.
topics.pro: A sort key defines the comparison used to order rows; equal keys keep an unspecified relative order unless a tie-breaker is added.
points: One key is enough for simple reports.
Equal keys need a tie-breaker.
The result is only guaranteed when the order is total.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks;

topics.title: ASC
topics.simple: ASC ascending order me sort karta hai — chhota se bada.
topics.pro: ASC is the default sort direction and orders values from smallest to largest, or A to Z for text.
points: ASC is optional.
Numbers go low to high.
Text follows the collation.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks ASC;

topics.title: DESC
topics.simple: DESC descending order me sort karta hai — bada se chhota.
topics.pro: DESC orders values from largest to smallest, or Z to A for text.
points: DESC reverses the comparison.
It is not a stable sort by itself.
Add a tie-breaker for deterministic pages.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Sorting Numeric Data
topics.simple: Numbers natural numeric order me sort hote hain, text order me nahi.
topics.pro: Numeric columns sort by value, so 9 comes before 10; storing numbers as text would sort 10 before 9.
points: Use numeric types for numeric sorting.
Text sort is lexicographic.
Casting text to numeric changes the order.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Sorting Text Data
topics.simple: Text sort collation par depend karta hai; case aur language order badal sakta hai.
topics.pro: Text ordering follows the column collation, which controls case and locale rules; use LOWER() or a case-insensitive collation when needed.
points: A and a may sort differently by collation.
Use LOWER(name) for case-insensitive order.
Use a deterministic tie-breaker.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY LOWER(name);

topics.title: Sorting Date Values
topics.simple: Dates chronological order me sort hoti hain.
topics.pro: Date and timestamp values sort chronologically; DESC gives newest first.
points: Earlier dates come first in ASC.
DESC gives the latest first.
Timestamps include time within the day.

example.sql: SELECT student_id, enrolled_on FROM enrollments ORDER BY enrolled_on DESC;

topics.title: Multiple Sort Keys
topics.simple: Pehla key main order deta hai, doosra key ties todta hai.
topics.pro: Multiple ORDER BY expressions are applied left to right: the first is primary, later keys break ties.
points: Separate keys with commas.
Each key has its own direction.
The last key should make the order deterministic.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST, name ASC;
example.output: Highest known marks first, ties alphabetical.

topics.title: Sorting by Aliases and Expressions
topics.simple: ORDER BY alias ya expression use kar sakta hai.
topics.pro: ORDER BY can reference a select-list alias or repeat an expression, because it is evaluated after SELECT.
points: Aliases work in ORDER BY.
Expressions can be sorted directly.
Aliases do not work in WHERE.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks * 2 AS doubled FROM students ORDER BY doubled DESC;
example.output: Rows ordered by the doubled value.

topics.title: NULL Sorting
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me ASC default NULLs last, DESC default NULLs first.
topics.pro: By default PostgreSQL treats NULL as larger than any non-null value: ASC places NULLs last and DESC places them first; NULLS FIRST/LAST overrides it.
points: ASC default: NULLS LAST.
DESC default: NULLS FIRST.
Be explicit in reports.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks ASC NULLS LAST;
example.output: Known marks ascending, NULL marks last.

topics.title: LIMIT
topics.simple: LIMIT result ki maximum row count set karta hai.
topics.pro: LIMIT caps the number of rows returned after sorting; LIMIT without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary subset.
points: LIMIT 0 returns no rows.
LIMIT ALL means no limit.
Use ORDER BY for meaningful top-N.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 3;

topics.title: OFFSET
topics.simple: OFFSET starting rows skip karta hai.
topics.pro: OFFSET skips a number of rows after sorting and before the limit is applied.
points: OFFSET 0 is the first row.
Large offsets still scan skipped rows.
Use with ORDER BY for stable pages.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 3 OFFSET 3;

topics.title: Pagination
topics.simple: Pagination me page size aur page number se LIMIT/OFFSET nikalte hain.
topics.pro: A page uses LIMIT page_size OFFSET (page - 1) * page_size, with a deterministic ORDER BY so rows do not shift between pages.
points: Page 1 uses OFFSET 0.
Page 3 with size 10 uses OFFSET 20.
Always add a unique tie-breaker.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20;

topics.title: Top N Records
topics.simple: Top N ke liye ORDER BY DESC aur LIMIT N use karo.
topics.pro: Top-N queries sort by the ranking key descending and cap the result; ties need an explicit tie-breaker or a window function for exact semantics.
points: ORDER BY the ranking key.
LIMIT N caps the rows.
Ties can make the cut arbitrary.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5;

topics.title: Bottom N Records
topics.simple: Bottom N ke liye ascending order aur LIMIT use karo.
topics.pro: Bottom-N queries sort ascending and cap the result; NULL placement can affect what counts as the bottom.
points: ASC gives the smallest first.
NULLS LAST keeps unknown values out of the bottom.
Add a tie-breaker for stability.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks ASC NULLS LAST LIMIT 5;

topics.title: Deterministic Ordering
topics.simple: Deterministic order ke liye unique tie-breaker add karo.
topics.pro: A total ordering uses a unique key as the final sort expression, so equal values cannot swap between pages or runs.
points: Add id as the last key.
Without it, LIMIT can change between runs.
Stable pages need a total order.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC;
example.output: Marks descending, NULLs last, id breaking every tie.

topics.title: Positional ORDER BY
topics.simple: ORDER BY 2 select list ke doosre column ko refer karta hai.
topics.pro: ORDER BY can use a select-list position, but positional references are fragile when the projection changes and should be avoided in application SQL.
points: Position 1 is the first output column.
It breaks when columns are reordered.
Prefer explicit names or aliases.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students ORDER BY 2 DESC;
example.output: Rows ordered by marks, the second column.

topics.title: ORDER BY with WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE pehle filter karta hai, phir ORDER BY sort karta hai.
topics.pro: Logical evaluation filters rows in WHERE, projects them in SELECT, then sorts the surviving rows in ORDER BY.
points: WHERE runs before ORDER BY.
Sorting only the filtered rows is cheaper.
LIMIT applies last.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks >= 60 ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: Sorting Performance
topics.simple: Bade result ko sort karna costly hota hai; index madad kar sakta hai.
topics.pro: A sort may use memory or disk; a matching B-tree index can return rows already ordered and avoid a sort for prefix-ordered queries.
points: Watch EXPLAIN for Sort nodes.
Indexes help matching ORDER BY prefixes.
Large OFFSET still skips rows.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 10;
example.output: An Index Scan or a Sort depending on available indexes.

topics.title: Practical Ranking Report
topics.simple: Ab filter, sort, tie-breaker aur limit mila kar ranking report banao.
topics.pro: A reliable ranking report combines a filter, a deterministic ORDER BY, an explicit NULL policy and a LIMIT, and is reviewed with EXPLAIN when it grows.
points: Filter first.
Sort by the ranking key.
Break ties with id.
Cap the report with LIMIT.

example.sql: SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks IS NOT NULL ORDER BY marks DESC, id ASC LIMIT 10;
example.output: Top ten known marks with stable ties.

interview.q: Can ORDER BY use an alias?
interview.answer: Yes, because ORDER BY is evaluated after SELECT.

interview.q: Can WHERE use a SELECT alias?
interview.answer: No, because WHERE runs before SELECT.

interview.q: How does PostgreSQL sort NULLs by default?
interview.answer: As larger than non-null values: NULLS LAST for ASC and NULLS FIRST for DESC.

interview.q: How do you force NULLs last?
interview.answer: Add NULLS LAST to the ORDER BY expression.

interview.q: What does LIMIT do?
interview.answer: Caps the number of rows returned after sorting.

interview.q: What does OFFSET do?
interview.answer: Skips a number of rows before the limit is applied.

interview.q: How do you calculate a pagination offset?
interview.answer: Offset = (page - 1) × page_size, with page 1 at offset 0.

interview.q: Why is LIMIT without ORDER BY unsafe?
interview.answer: The database may return any subset because no row order is guaranteed.

interview.q: Why is a tie-breaker important for pagination?
interview.answer: Equal sort keys can swap between pages; a unique final key makes the order total.

interview.q: What is top-N SQL?
interview.answer: ORDER BY ranking_key DESC LIMIT n, with a tie-breaker for stable results.

interview.q: What is the difference between LIMIT and FETCH FIRST?
interview.answer: LIMIT is PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQLite syntax; FETCH FIRST is standard SQL and also supported by PostgreSQL.

interview.q: Why can a large OFFSET be slow?
interview.answer: The database still has to scan and discard the skipped rows.

interview.q: What is keyset pagination?
interview.answer: Paginating by a stable key, such as WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT n, instead of skipping a large offset.

interview.q: How can an index help ORDER BY?
interview.answer: A B-tree index matching the sort prefix can return rows already ordered and avoid a sort.

interview.q: Why does text sort vary?
interview.answer: Text ordering follows the collation, which controls case and locale rules.

interview.q: Can ORDER BY use an expression?
interview.answer: Yes, including functions and arithmetic, but the expression must be evaluated for each row.

logic.q: Why is ORDER BY without LIMIT potentially expensive?
logic.answer: The database may sort the entire result before returning any rows.

logic.q: Why is LIMIT without ORDER BY arbitrary?
logic.answer: There is no guaranteed row order, so any subset may be chosen.

logic.q: Why add a unique tie-breaker?
logic.answer: Equal sort keys can swap between runs and pages; a unique final key makes the order total.

logic.q: Why does ASC put NULLs last in PostgreSQL?
logic.answer: NULL sorts as larger than any non-null value in the default ordering.

logic.q: Why does DESC put NULLs first?
logic.answer: DESC reverses the default ordering, so the largest value (NULL) comes first.

logic.q: Why can text sorting surprise you?
logic.answer: Collation controls case and locale rules, so A and a may not sort as expected.

logic.q: Why does a large OFFSET get slower?
logic.answer: The server still scans and discards every skipped row.

logic.q: Why is keyset pagination often faster?
logic.answer: It seeks directly after the last key instead of counting and discarding rows.

logic.q: Why does an alias work in ORDER BY but not WHERE?
logic.answer: ORDER BY runs after SELECT defines the alias; WHERE runs before it.

logic.q: Why is positional ORDER BY fragile?
logic.answer: Changing the select list reorders or removes the referenced position.

logic.q: Why does WHERE run before ORDER BY?
logic.answer: Filtering first reduces the rows that must be sorted.

logic.q: Why does SELECT DISTINCT restrict ORDER BY expressions?
logic.answer: For DISTINCT, ORDER BY expressions must appear in the select list so the sort is defined on the projected rows.

logic.q: Why can an index satisfy ORDER BY?
logic.answer: A B-tree index matching the sort prefix returns rows in the requested order without a separate sort.

logic.q: Why does LIMIT apply after ORDER BY?
logic.answer: The rows must be ordered before the first N can be chosen.

logic.q: Why is ORDER BY random() expensive?
logic.answer: It computes a random value for every row and sorts the whole set with no useful index.

modules.title: UPDATE, DELETE and Data Modification
modules.goal: Modify and remove rows safely, with verification and rollback.

topics.title: What Is UPDATE?
topics.simple: UPDATE existing rows ke values badalta hai.
topics.pro: UPDATE is DML that changes column values for rows matched by an optional WHERE clause and returns a count of affected rows.
points: UPDATE changes data, not structure.
Without WHERE it targets every row.
The statement is atomic.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: UPDATE Syntax
topics.simple: Basic shape: UPDATE table SET column = value WHERE condition.
topics.pro: The syntax is UPDATE table SET column = expression [, ...] [FROM ...] [WHERE ...] [RETURNING ...].
points: SET lists assignments separated by commas.
WHERE limits the target rows.
RETURNING returns changed rows.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav S' WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating One Column
topics.simple: Ek column ki value badalne ke liye ek assignment likho.
topics.pro: A single-column UPDATE assigns one expression to one column for every matched row.
points: Use the primary key in WHERE for a single row.
The new value must satisfy the column type.
Check the affected count.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Multiple columns ko comma se update karo.
topics.pro: Multiple assignments run in one statement; all expressions see the row values from before the statement, not the just-assigned values.
points: Separate assignments with commas.
Assignments are evaluated from the old row.
The whole statement is atomic.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET name = 'Aarav S', marks = 90 WHERE id = 1;

topics.title: Updating Specific Rows
topics.simple: WHERE se sirf intended rows update karo.
topics.pro: A WHERE predicate targets specific rows; a unique key gives the smallest and safest target.
points: Match on a key when possible.
Preview the rows with SELECT.
Check the reported row count.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 88 WHERE id = 2;

topics.title: UPDATE with WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE ke bina UPDATE poore table ko chhu sakta hai.
topics.pro: WHERE filters the target rows before assignment; omitting it updates every row in the table.
points: No WHERE means every row.
Use IS NULL for null checks.
Test the predicate with SELECT first.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 0 WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with Expressions
topics.simple: New value purani value par calculation ho sakti hai.
topics.pro: The SET expression can reference existing columns, arithmetic, functions and CASE, and is evaluated for each matched row.
points: marks + 5 uses the old marks.
CASE handles conditional updates.
The result must fit the column type.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks IS NOT NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with CASE and COALESCE
topics.simple: CASE conditional value deta hai; COALESCE fallback deta hai.
topics.pro: CASE chooses a value per row, while COALESCE replaces NULL with a fallback; both are common in data-repair updates.
points: CASE avoids separate statements.
COALESCE fills missing values.
Both are evaluated per row.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET email = COALESCE(email, 'unknown@example.com');

topics.title: UPDATE with Subquery
topics.simple: Subquery se naya value compute kar sakte hain.
topics.pro: A scalar subquery in SET must return at most one row and one column; a multi-row result raises an error.
points: The subquery must be scalar.
A NULL subquery result assigns NULL.
Test the subquery separately.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: UPDATE with FROM
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me UPDATE FROM doosri table se values laata hai.
topics.pro: UPDATE ... FROM joins the target to a source relation; each target row should match at most one source row to keep the result deterministic.
points: FROM adds a source table.
Join in WHERE.
Duplicate source matches make the update unpredictable.

example.sql: UPDATE students s SET marks = a.marks FROM applicants a WHERE s.email = a.email;

topics.title: RETURNING with UPDATE
topics.simple: RETURNING updated rows wapas deta hai.
topics.pro: RETURNING returns the new row values for every updated row, including generated values and expressions.
points: RETURNING is PostgreSQL syntax.
It shows exactly what changed.
It can return old values only via a CTE or trigger.

example.sql: UPDATE students SET marks = 95 WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id, name, marks;

topics.title: What Is DELETE?
topics.simple: DELETE rows ko table se hataata hai.
topics.pro: DELETE is DML that removes rows matched by WHERE and returns the number deleted.
points: DELETE keeps the table structure.
Without WHERE it removes every row.
It fires row-level DELETE triggers.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 3;

topics.title: DELETE Syntax
topics.simple: Basic shape: DELETE FROM table WHERE condition.
topics.pro: The syntax is DELETE FROM table [USING ...] [WHERE ...] [RETURNING ...].
points: FROM names the target table.
WHERE limits the rows.
RETURNING shows removed rows.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60;

topics.title: DELETE Specific Rows
topics.simple: WHERE se specific row delete karo.
topics.pro: A precise predicate deletes only the intended rows; a primary key is the safest target.
points: Preview with SELECT.
Use a key when possible.
Check the affected count.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 4;

topics.title: DELETE with Conditions
topics.simple: Range, list aur NULL conditions delete me bhi kaam karte hain.
topics.pro: DELETE accepts the same boolean predicates as SELECT, including comparisons, IN, LIKE and IS NULL.
points: Use IS NULL for null checks.
BETWEEN and IN work normally.
One statement is atomic.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks IS NULL;

topics.title: DELETE with Subquery
topics.simple: Subquery se decide kar sakte hain kaunse rows delete honge.
topics.pro: DELETE with IN or EXISTS uses a subquery to choose rows; beware NOT IN with NULLs, which can match nothing.
points: IN works for a list of keys.
NOT EXISTS is safer with NULLs.
The subquery must be correct before deleting.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

topics.title: DELETE with USING
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me DELETE USING doosri table se join karke rows delete karta hai.
topics.pro: DELETE ... USING adds source relations to the WHERE join, removing target rows that match the source.
points: USING is PostgreSQL syntax.
Join the target and source in WHERE.
A row is deleted at most once.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students s USING enrollments e WHERE s.id = e.student_id AND e.course_id = 10;

topics.title: RETURNING with DELETE
topics.simple: RETURNING deleted rows ko wapas deta hai — archive ke liye useful.
topics.pro: RETURNING returns the deleted row values, which can be inserted into an archive table in the same statement.
points: Return the rows before they disappear.
Combine with a CTE to archive.
RETURNING does not prevent the delete.

example.sql: DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING id, name, marks;

topics.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE
topics.simple: DELETE filtered aur trigger-friendly hai; TRUNCATE poora table jaldi khali karta hai.
topics.pro: DELETE removes selected rows, fires row triggers and is transactional; TRUNCATE removes all rows, has no WHERE, does not fire row DELETE triggers and is transactional in PostgreSQL.
points: DELETE supports WHERE.
TRUNCATE has no WHERE.
TRUNCATE resets storage; RESTART IDENTITY resets sequences.

example.sql: TRUNCATE TABLE students RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE;

topics.title: Safe Modification Practices and Common Errors
topics.simple: Bade UPDATE/DELETE se pehle SELECT, transaction aur row count check karo.
topics.pro: Safe modification means previewing the target rows, wrapping the change in a transaction, checking the affected count and using RETURNING or a backup before committing.
points: Preview with SELECT.
Use BEGIN and verify.
Commit only after the count matches.
Use RETURNING for an audit trail.

interview.q: What is UPDATE?
interview.answer: DML that changes column values for rows matched by WHERE and returns the affected count.

interview.q: What is DELETE?
interview.answer: DML that removes rows matched by WHERE and returns the deleted count.

interview.q: What happens without WHERE in UPDATE or DELETE?
interview.answer: The statement targets every row in the table.

interview.q: How do multiple SET assignments evaluate?
interview.answer: All expressions read the row values from before the statement, not values assigned earlier in the same SET list.

interview.q: How do you update from another table in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Use UPDATE ... FROM source WHERE join_condition; each target row should match at most one source row.

interview.q: How do you delete using another table in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Use DELETE FROM target USING source WHERE join_condition; each target row is deleted at most once.

interview.q: What does RETURNING do?
interview.answer: Returns the changed or deleted rows in the same statement.

interview.q: What is a scalar subquery?
interview.answer: A subquery that returns at most one row and one column, usable where a single value is expected.

interview.q: What happens if a SET subquery returns multiple rows?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL raises an error because the subquery is not scalar.

interview.q: What is the difference between DELETE and TRUNCATE?
interview.answer: DELETE supports WHERE, fires row triggers and removes selected rows; TRUNCATE removes all rows, has no WHERE, does not fire row DELETE triggers and resets storage.

interview.q: Is TRUNCATE transactional in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: Yes, it can be rolled back there; MySQL performs an implicit commit.

interview.q: Does DELETE reset identity?
interview.answer: No; use TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY or reset the sequence explicitly.

interview.q: How do you archive deleted rows?
interview.answer: Use DELETE ... RETURNING inside a CTE and insert the returned rows into an archive table.

interview.q: Why is DELETE with NOT IN and NULL dangerous?
interview.answer: The NULL comparison makes the predicate unknown, so no rows may be deleted; NOT EXISTS is safer.

interview.q: Why can a foreign key block DELETE?
interview.answer: Child rows still reference the parent and the constraint has no cascade action.

interview.q: What happens if UPDATE changes a primary key?
interview.answer: It can break foreign keys or fail on duplicates; use ON UPDATE CASCADE only when the relationship requires it.

interview.q: Why use a transaction around a large modification?
interview.answer: It lets you verify the affected count and roll back cleanly if the change is wrong.

interview.q: Why can a large UPDATE be expensive?
interview.answer: It creates new row versions, writes WAL, updates indexes and can bloat the table until vacuum runs.

interview.q: Why can a large DELETE be expensive?
interview.answer: It creates dead tuples, writes WAL and must maintain indexes; batching reduces lock time.

interview.q: What is the safest modification workflow?
interview.answer: Preview with SELECT, open a transaction, run the change with RETURNING, verify the count, then commit or roll back.

logic.q: Why preview with SELECT first?

logic.q: Why wrap a modification in a transaction?
logic.answer: You can verify the affected count and roll back if the change is wrong.

logic.q: Why use RETURNING?
logic.answer: It shows the changed rows and supports an audit or archive without a second query.

logic.q: Why does DELETE support WHERE but TRUNCATE does not?
logic.answer: DELETE removes selected rows one by one; TRUNCATE is a whole-table storage operation.

logic.q: Why does DELETE fire row triggers but TRUNCATE does not?
logic.answer: DELETE processes rows individually; TRUNCATE does not visit them as row deletes.

logic.q: Why is changing a primary key risky?
logic.answer: Foreign keys reference the old value; without ON UPDATE CASCADE the change can fail or orphan relationships.

logic.q: Why must a SET subquery be scalar?
logic.answer: A column assignment needs one value per row; multiple rows cannot fit.

logic.q: Why can UPDATE FROM be unpredictable with duplicate sources?
logic.answer: A target row matched by several source rows may be updated more than once with no defined winner.

logic.q: Why is NOT IN with a NULL subquery unsafe for DELETE?

logic.q: Why can a foreign key block DELETE?
