modules.title: Joins
modules.goal: Combine related tables correctly and choose the join type by which rows must survive.

topics.title: Introduction to Joins
topics.simple: Join do tables ko ek related result me combine karta hai.
topics.pro: A join combines rows from two relations using a predicate, typically matching a foreign key to a primary key.
points: Joins combine columns from multiple tables.
The join key defines the relationship.
A missing join condition creates a cross product.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: Each student with their enrolled course ids.

topics.title: INNER JOIN
topics.simple: INNER JOIN sirf matching rows deta hai.
topics.pro: INNER JOIN returns only pairs where the ON condition is true; unmatched rows from either side disappear.
points: Only matches survive.
Non-matching rows are dropped.
Duplicate matches multiply rows.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s INNER JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: Students who have at least one enrollment.

topics.title: LEFT JOIN
topics.simple: LEFT JOIN left table ke saare rows rakhta hai.
topics.pro: LEFT JOIN preserves every row from the left relation and fills unmatched right columns with NULL.
points: All left rows survive.
Unmatched right columns are NULL.
Filtering the right table in WHERE can remove the preserved rows.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: Every student, with NULL course_id when unenrolled.

topics.title: RIGHT JOIN
topics.simple: RIGHT JOIN right table ke saare rows rakhta hai.
topics.pro: RIGHT JOIN preserves every row from the right relation and fills unmatched left columns with NULL; it is a mirrored LEFT JOIN.
points: All right rows survive.
Unmatched left columns are NULL.
Prefer LEFT JOIN for readability.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM enrollments e RIGHT JOIN students s ON s.id = e.student_id;

topics.title: FULL OUTER JOIN
topics.simple: FULL JOIN dono tables ke saare rows rakhta hai.
topics.pro: FULL OUTER JOIN returns matched rows plus unmatched rows from both sides, with NULLs on the missing side.
points: Both sides are preserved.
Use COALESCE to pick a non-null key.
It is the union of LEFT and RIGHT joins.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s FULL OUTER JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id;
example.output: Every student and every enrollment, matched where possible.

topics.title: CROSS JOIN
topics.simple: CROSS JOIN har left row ko har right row se pair karta hai.
topics.pro: CROSS JOIN produces the Cartesian product: every row from the first relation paired with every row from the second.
points: Rows multiply: left × right.
There is no ON condition.
Accidental cross joins are expensive.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s CROSS JOIN courses c;

topics.title: SELF JOIN
topics.simple: Self join ek hi table ko do aliases se join karta hai.
topics.pro: A self join uses two aliases for the same table so rows can be compared with other rows in that table.
points: Both copies need aliases.
The ON condition defines the relationship.
It is common for hierarchies and comparisons.

example.sql: SELECT a.name AS lower, b.name AS higher FROM students a JOIN students b ON a.marks < b.marks;
example.output: Pairs where the first student scored lower.

topics.title: Join Conditions
topics.simple: ON join ka matching rule likhta hai.
topics.pro: ON defines the boolean condition that decides which row pairs are joined; it is required for INNER and OUTER joins unless USING is used.
points: ON belongs to the join.
It can include extra predicates.
A wrong key silently produces wrong rows.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: One row per matching student-enrollment pair.

topics.title: Joining on Multiple Columns
topics.simple: Composite key ko ON me AND se match karo.
topics.pro: When the relationship uses a composite key, every key column must appear in the join condition.
points: Match all key columns.
Missing one column multiplies matches.
Use AND between key predicates.

example.sql: SELECT e.student_id, cs.room FROM enrollments e JOIN course_sections cs ON cs.course_id = e.course_id AND cs.semester = e.semester;
example.output: Enrollments matched to their section room.

topics.title: Joining Multiple Tables
topics.simple: Ek query me teen ya zyada tables chain ki tarah join hoti hain.
topics.pro: Multi-table joins chain relationships: each new JOIN adds a relation and an ON condition connecting it to the existing result.
points: Add one join per relationship.
Join on indexed keys.
Check row counts after each added table.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id;

topics.title: Table Aliases
topics.simple: Aliases lambi table names ko short aur readable banate hain.
topics.pro: Aliases give each relation a short name used to qualify columns and are mandatory when the same table appears twice.
points: Alias after the table name.
Qualify columns with the alias.
Self joins require distinct aliases.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students AS s JOIN enrollments AS e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses AS c ON c.id = e.course_id;

topics.title: Ambiguous Columns
topics.simple: Same column name do tables me ho to qualify karo.
topics.pro: If a column name exists in more than one joined relation, an unqualified reference is ambiguous and PostgreSQL raises an error.
points: Qualify with the table alias.
Do not rely on column order.
Alias every joined table.

example.sql: SELECT s.id, s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id;
example.output: Student id and name plus course title.

topics.title: JOIN vs Subquery
topics.simple: JOIN columns combine karta hai; subquery value ya membership deta hai.
topics.pro: A join returns columns from both relations, while a subquery is often used for a scalar value, IN membership or EXISTS existence checks.
points: JOIN is natural for output columns.
EXISTS is natural for existence.
Semi-joins avoid duplicate output rows.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);
example.output: Students enrolled in course 10, once each.

topics.title: JOIN with Aggregation
topics.simple: Join ke baad GROUP BY se counts nikal sakte hain.
topics.pro: Joining and grouping lets you aggregate related rows; LEFT JOIN plus COUNT(right_key) reports zero for rows with no match.
points: GROUP BY the non-aggregated columns.
COUNT(right_key) counts matches.
COUNT(*) counts the preserved row too.

example.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title;
example.output: Every course with its enrollment count, including zero.

topics.title: JOIN with Filtering
topics.simple: Filter join ke baad WHERE se hota hai.
topics.pro: WHERE filters the joined result; for INNER JOIN it is equivalent to putting the predicate in ON, but for OUTER JOIN the placement changes which rows survive.
points: WHERE filters the final rows.
ON filters the match.
Placement matters for outer joins.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE c.credits = 3;

topics.title: ON vs WHERE in Outer Joins
topics.simple: LEFT JOIN me right-table filter ON me rakho, WHERE me nahi.
topics.pro: A predicate on the right table in ON filters only the match, preserving left rows; the same predicate in WHERE removes non-matching left rows and turns the join into an inner join.
points: ON keeps the outer join.
WHERE can remove preserved rows.
This is a common reporting bug.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id AND e.course_id = 10;
example.output: Every student, with course 10 only where enrolled.

topics.title: Anti-Joins and Missing Rows
topics.simple: Anti-join un rows ko dhoondhta hai jinka match nahi hai.
topics.pro: A LEFT JOIN with WHERE right_key IS NULL, or a NOT EXISTS subquery, returns rows with no matching row on the other side.
points: LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL is an anti-join.
NOT EXISTS is usually clearer.
Avoid NOT IN when NULLs are possible.

example.sql: SELECT s.name FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id WHERE e.student_id IS NULL;

topics.title: Common Join Errors
topics.simple: Missing ON, wrong key aur duplicate matches sabse common join bugs hain.
topics.pro: Most join bugs come from a missing or wrong join condition, an ambiguous column, a filter in the wrong clause or a one-to-many relationship that multiplies rows.
points: Every join needs a condition.
Qualify shared column names.
Check the row count before aggregating.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, e.course_id FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id;
example.output: One row per enrollment, not one per student.

topics.title: Join Performance
topics.simple: Join keys par index aur selective filters performance decide karte hain.
topics.pro: The planner chooses nested loop, hash or merge join based on statistics, indexes and selectivity; indexes on foreign keys and selective WHERE predicates usually help most.
points: Index the join keys.
Filter early and selectively.
Read EXPLAIN plans.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT s.name, c.title FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id JOIN courses c ON c.id = e.course_id WHERE c.id = 10;
example.output: A plan showing the chosen join strategy.

topics.title: Practical Join Examples
topics.simple: Ab joins ko real reports me combine karo.
topics.pro: Practical join work combines the right join type, a correct condition, a filter and an aggregate, and verifies the grain of the result before trusting it.
points: Choose the join type by which rows must survive.
State the output grain.
Check counts and NULLs.
Review the plan for large joins.

example.sql: SELECT c.title, COUNT(e.student_id) AS enrolled FROM courses c LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.course_id = c.id GROUP BY c.id, c.title ORDER BY enrolled DESC, c.title ASC;

interview.q: What is a join?
interview.answer: An operation that combines rows from two relations using a matching condition.

interview.q: What is a join key?
interview.answer: The column or columns used to match rows, usually a foreign key to a primary key.

interview.q: What is the difference between INNER and LEFT JOIN?
interview.answer: INNER keeps only matches; LEFT keeps every left row and NULL-fills unmatched right columns.

interview.q: What is the difference between LEFT and RIGHT JOIN?
interview.answer: They preserve opposite sides; a RIGHT JOIN is a mirrored LEFT JOIN.

interview.q: What is a FULL OUTER JOIN?
interview.answer: A join that preserves unmatched rows from both sides, NULL-filling the missing side.

interview.q: What is a CROSS JOIN?
interview.answer: The Cartesian product: every row from one relation paired with every row from the other.

interview.q: When do you use a self join?
interview.answer: When rows in one table must be compared with other rows in the same table, such as hierarchies or pairs.

interview.q: What is the difference between ON and WHERE in an outer join?
interview.answer: ON filters the match while preserving the outer side; WHERE filters the final rows and can remove preserved rows.

interview.q: What does USING do?
interview.answer: It joins on same-named columns and outputs one copy of the join column.

interview.q: Why is NATURAL JOIN risky?
interview.answer: It joins on every same-named column, so a schema change can silently change the condition.

interview.q: How do you find rows with no match?
interview.answer: Use LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right_key IS NULL or NOT EXISTS.

interview.q: Why is NOT IN risky for an anti-join?
interview.answer: A NULL in the subquery makes the predicate unknown and can return no rows.

interview.q: What is the grain of a joined result?
interview.answer: What one output row represents, such as one student-course pair; a one-to-many join changes the grain.

interview.q: Why can COUNT(*) differ from COUNT(right_key) after a LEFT JOIN?
interview.answer: COUNT(*) counts the preserved row even when the right side is NULL; COUNT(right_key) counts only real matches.

interview.q: How do you join multiple tables?
interview.answer: Chain JOIN clauses, adding one relation and its ON condition for each relationship.

interview.q: What are the main join algorithms?
interview.answer: Nested loop, hash join and merge join; the planner chooses based on statistics, indexes and selectivity.

interview.q: Why qualify columns in a join?
interview.answer: Shared column names are ambiguous, and qualification documents which table a value comes from.

interview.q: Can a join use a non-unique key?
interview.answer: Yes, but each matching pair becomes a row, so the result can multiply.

interview.q: How do you join on a composite key?
interview.answer: Put every key column in the ON condition, combined with AND.

interview.q: Does join order in SQL determine execution order?
interview.answer: No; the planner may reorder joins while preserving the result.

logic.q: When should you use INNER JOIN instead of LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: When only rows with matches are meaningful and unmatched rows should be excluded.

logic.q: When should you use LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: When every row from the left side must appear, even without a match.

logic.q: Why is RIGHT JOIN often rewritten as LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: Swapping the table order makes the preserved side the left side, which is easier to read.

logic.q: Why use FULL OUTER JOIN?
logic.answer: When unmatched rows from both sides matter, such as reconciling two systems.

logic.q: Why is a CROSS JOIN dangerous by accident?
logic.answer: It multiplies every row by every row, producing a huge result and misleading aggregates.

logic.q: Why does a self join need aliases?
logic.answer: The same table appears twice, so aliases distinguish the two row roles.

logic.q: Why does a right-table filter in WHERE break a LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: The WHERE predicate rejects NULL right-side rows, removing the preserved left rows.

logic.q: Why can NULL join keys fail to match?
logic.answer: Equality with NULL is unknown, so NULL = NULL is not true.

logic.q: Why can a one-to-many join inflate a SUM?
logic.answer: A parent row repeated for each child is summed once per child, not once per parent.

logic.q: Why is COUNT(*) different after a LEFT JOIN?
logic.answer: It counts the preserved row even when the right side has no match.

logic.q: Why prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN for anti-joins?
logic.answer: NOT EXISTS handles NULLs predictably; NOT IN with a NULL can return no rows.

logic.q: Why use a join instead of a subquery?
logic.answer: A join returns columns from both tables; a subquery is often better for a scalar or an existence check.

logic.q: Why index foreign keys?
logic.answer: The planner can find matching rows without scanning the child table repeatedly.

logic.q: Does the written join order control execution?
logic.answer: No; the planner can reorder joins while preserving the result.

logic.q: Why is NATURAL JOIN fragile?
logic.answer: It silently joins on every same-named column, so schema changes alter the condition.
